The problem

## Why does my tailbone hurt when I sit?

The coccyx, or tailbone, is the small bone at the very bottom of your spine. Every time you sit, and especially when you lean back, part of your weight rests on it. If it has been bruised, strained or pushed out of position by a fall, childbirth or long hours of sitting, that pressure turns into pain. Doctors call this **coccydynia**.

### Does this sound familiar?

- Pain right at the base of the spine

- Worse the longer you sit, or when you lean back

- A sharp jolt when you get up from a chair

- Pain during bowel movements or intercourse

The good news: it is very treatable, and surgery is rarely needed.

Why sitting hurts: leaning back loads the coccyx; leaning slightly forward moves your weight onto the sitting bones.

# Coccydynia (tailbone pain): symptoms, causes and self-check

Understanding coccydynia

## A small bone that can take over your whole day.

The coccyx is the last few small vertebrae at the base of your spine. It carries part of your weight every time you sit and anchors several muscles, tendons and ligaments of the pelvic floor. When it's injured, inflamed or out of position, the pain is called **coccydynia**.

It often follows a fall onto the backside, childbirth, long hours on hard seats, or repetitive strain like cycling or rowing. Sometimes there's no clear cause. Either way, it is treatable, and it rarely needs surgery.

🛝 Falls & direct trauma
🤰 Pregnancy & childbirth
💺 Prolonged sitting
🚴 Repetitive strain
⚖️ Sudden weight change
❔ No obvious cause

### Quick symptom check

Tick everything that sounds familiar. This is not a diagnosis, just a guide to whether a specialist consult makes sense.

Pain right at the bottom of the spine
It hurts more the longer I sit
Sharp pain when standing up from a chair
Leaning forward or to one side when sitting helps
Pain during bowel movements
Pain during intercourse or periods
Lying on my back is uncomfortable
I had a fall, injury or childbirth before it started

Select the symptoms that apply to you.

[Talk to a specialist](https://tailbone.netlify.app/book)

Medical facts

## What doctors know about tailbone pain

A plain-language summary based on leading medical references. It is general information and not a substitute for an examination.

### How common is it?

Tailbone pain is common. Women are affected around five times as often as men, partly because of pregnancy, childbirth and the shape of the pelvis. It is unusual in children.

### Usual causes

- A fall onto the backside, or another injury

- Pregnancy and childbirth

- Long hours sitting, especially on hard seats or while driving

- Repetitive strain, such as cycling or rowing

- Being well above or below a healthy weight; very flexible or very stiff joints

- Sometimes no clear cause is found

### Typical symptoms

- Aching or sharp pain at the very base of the spine

- Worse when sitting, leaning back, or getting up from a chair

- Pain with bowel movements or during intercourse

- Poor sleep and low mood when it lasts

### How it is diagnosed

Mainly through your history and a careful examination of the coccyx and surrounding muscles. Imaging is used when needed: X-rays (sometimes taken sitting and standing) for fractures or an unstable coccyx, and MRI to look for inflammation or other causes.

### Treatment options

- **Self-care:** a coccyx cushion, good posture with lower-back support, heat or ice, avoiding long sitting, softer stools

- **Hands-on therapy:** physiotherapy, pelvic-floor work and manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles

- **Injections:** local anaesthetic with steroid, when other measures don't help

- **Surgery** (removing part or all of the coccyx) is rare and kept for cases where everything else has failed

### Outlook

Most people improve within weeks with the right care. Pain that lasts more than a few weeks, or keeps coming back, deserves a specialist assessment rather than "just living with it".

### ⚠️ See a doctor promptly if tailbone pain comes with:

- Fever or feeling unwell

- Numbness, tingling or weakness in the legs or around the buttocks

- New problems controlling your bladder or bowels

- A lump, swelling or wound near the tailbone

- Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer

- Severe pain after a major accident

For sudden numbness around the buttocks or loss of bladder or bowel control, go to an emergency department straight away.

### Sources and further reading

- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain) ↗

- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/) ↗

Summarised in our own words for patients. Links open the original pages; we are not affiliated with these organisations.

# Tailbone pain: frequently asked questions

FAQ

## Questions patients often ask.

### What is coccydynia?

It's the medical name for pain in and around the coccyx (tailbone). It usually gets worse when sitting, especially when leaning back, and when standing up after sitting.

### What is Internal Manipulation, and does it hurt?

It's a hands-on, non-surgical technique that frees up the tight ligaments and muscles attached to the coccyx and restores its alignment and movement. It is quick and done with full consent and privacy. Patients commonly report it's far less uncomfortable than they expected.

### How many sessions will I need?

It depends on your diagnosis, how long you've had the pain and your general health. Some people need very few visits, and others need a short course. We reassess your progress at every visit.

### What should I bring to my appointment?

A short note of how and when the pain started, any past injuries or operations, and a list of the medicines you take. Wear comfortable clothing.

### Do I need a referral from a doctor?

No. You can book directly with us by phone, WhatsApp or the form above.

Yes. A female specialist trained by Dr Rajveer Singh is available. Just mention it when you book.

# Sitting with tailbone pain: 8 practical ways to ease it

Desk job, long drives or a hard classroom bench? Small changes to how and how long you sit can take a lot of pressure off a sore coccyx.

If your tailbone hurts, sitting is usually the hardest part of the day. When you sit upright or lean back, part of your weight rests on the coccyx, the small bone at the very bottom of the spine. When it is bruised, inflamed or moving abnormally, that pressure turns into pain, and getting up from a chair can bring a sharp jolt.

The good news is that how you sit makes a real difference. These are the changes our patients find most useful.

## 1. Lean slightly forward

Tilting your upper body a little forward shifts your weight onto your thigh bones and the "sitting bones" of your pelvis, and off the coccyx. Sitting on the front half of the chair with your feet flat on the floor makes this easier.

## 2. Use a cut-out cushion

A wedge or U-shaped cushion with a gap at the back lets the tailbone hang free instead of pressing on the seat. Round "doughnut" rings help some people but can still press on the coccyx, so a cushion with an open back is usually better. Take it with you: to the office, the car and restaurants.

## 3. Choose firm seats over soft sofas

It sounds backwards, but deep, soft sofas let you sink and roll back onto the tailbone. A firm, supportive chair with a cushion is kinder.

## 4. Get up every 30 minutes

Pressure and stiffness build the longer you sit. Set a reminder to stand, walk a few steps or do a gentle stretch every half hour. On long drives, plan short breaks.

## 5. Stand up the smart way

Shift forward to the edge of the seat, bring your feet back under you, and push up through your legs while keeping your back straight. This avoids rocking back onto the coccyx at the moment you rise.

## 6. Support your lower back

A small cushion or rolled towel behind the lower back keeps you upright and stops you slumping, which tips weight back onto the tailbone.

## 7. Heat or ice

For a few minutes at a time, a warm pack can relax tight muscles around the coccyx, and an ice pack wrapped in a cloth can calm a flare-up. Use whichever helps you more.

## 8. Keep your bowels comfortable

Straining often makes tailbone pain worse. Plenty of water, fruit, vegetables and fibre help. If bowel movements are painful, ask your doctor or pharmacist about a gentle stool softener.

## When self-care isn't enough

Most tailbone pain settles with time and sensible habits. If yours hasn't improved after a few weeks, keeps coming back, or stops you working or sleeping, it is worth having the coccyx and surrounding muscles properly examined. A displaced or stiff coccyx, or tight pelvic-floor muscles, often needs hands-on treatment rather than more waiting.

See a doctor promptly if the pain comes with fever, numbness, leg weakness, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels.

## Sources

- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)
- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)

# Tailbone pain after pregnancy: why it happens and what helps

Many new mothers find that sitting to feed their baby is surprisingly painful. Here is why childbirth can affect the coccyx, and how it is treated.

Tailbone pain is much more common in women than in men, and pregnancy and childbirth are among the main reasons. Many mothers notice it in the weeks after delivery, often while sitting to feed the baby, which is exactly when sitting is hardest to avoid.

## Why pregnancy and childbirth affect the coccyx

- **Hormones loosen the joints.** During pregnancy, hormones relax the ligaments of the pelvis so the baby can pass through. The joint between the sacrum and the coccyx loosens too.
- **The baby's head presses on the coccyx** during a vaginal delivery, pushing it backwards. Occasionally the coccyx is bruised, strained or even displaced.
- **Weight and posture change.** Through pregnancy, the way you sit and stand changes, putting new strain on the lower spine and pelvic floor.
- **Assisted or long deliveries** and larger babies make injury a little more likely.

## What it typically feels like

- An ache or sharp pain right at the base of the spine
- Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and when standing up
- Sometimes painful bowel movements or discomfort during intercourse

## What helps

1. **A cut-out (wedge or U-shaped) cushion** for feeding and for the car.
2. **Feeding positions that take weight off the tailbone:** lying on your side, or sitting leaning slightly forward with good back support.
3. **Gentle pelvic-floor exercises** once your midwife or doctor says it is safe.
4. **Keeping stools soft:** fluids and fibre, and avoiding straining.
5. **Heat or cold packs** for short periods.

Before taking pain relief while breastfeeding, check with your doctor or pharmacist which medicines are suitable.

## When to get it checked

Postnatal tailbone pain often eases over a few weeks. If it lasts longer than that, keeps returning, or makes caring for your baby difficult, ask for an examination. When the coccyx has been pushed out of its normal position or the surrounding muscles stay in spasm, hands-on treatment can help a great deal, and you don't need to "just put up with it".

See a doctor urgently if you have fever, a wound or swelling near the tailbone, numbness, or new problems with bladder or bowel control.

## Sources

- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)
- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)

# Tailbone pain red flags: when it needs urgent attention

Most tailbone pain is mechanical and treatable without surgery. A few warning signs, though, mean you should see a doctor quickly. Here is what they are.

The vast majority of tailbone pain comes from a fall, childbirth, long sitting or strain on the coccyx and the muscles around it. It is uncomfortable and can be stubborn, but it isn't dangerous. Rarely, though, pain at the base of the spine is a sign of something that needs prompt medical care.

## See a doctor promptly if you have tailbone pain with:

- **Fever, chills or feeling generally unwell.** This could mean an infection, such as an abscess or an infected cyst near the tailbone (a pilonidal cyst).
- **A lump, swelling, redness or a wound** near the tailbone.
- **Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer.** Very occasionally, a growth in or near the sacrum or coccyx causes pain.
- **Pain that is severe and getting steadily worse**, or pain that is just as bad lying down at night.
- **Pain after a major accident** such as a road traffic collision or a fall from height, where a fracture is possible.

## Go to an emergency department straight away if you have:

- **Numbness around the buttocks, genitals or inner thighs** (sometimes called "saddle" numbness)
- **New difficulty passing urine, or loss of bladder or bowel control**
- **Weakness in one or both legs**

These can be signs of pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal, which needs urgent assessment.

## Why a proper examination matters

Because so many conditions can cause pain low in the back and pelvis, a specialist first takes a careful history and examines the coccyx, the joints around it and the pelvic muscles. When needed, X-rays taken sitting and standing can show whether the coccyx moves abnormally, and an MRI can rule out other causes. Only once the cause is clear should treatment begin.

If none of the warning signs above apply, tailbone pain is usually treatable with self-care and targeted, hands-on therapy. Surgery is rarely needed.

## Sources

- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)
- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)

# What happens at a coccydynia consultation (and how to prepare)

Nervous about your first visit for tailbone pain? Here is what to expect, step by step, and how to prepare so you get the most from the appointment.

Many people put off getting tailbone pain checked because they aren't sure what the visit involves, or they feel embarrassed. Knowing what happens makes it much easier.

## Before you come

- **Make a list of your medicines** and any past operations or injuries.
- **Note how your pain behaves:** when it started, what makes it worse (sitting, getting up, driving, bowel movements) and what helps.
- **Wear comfortable clothes.**
- If you would prefer to be seen by a **female clinician**, mention it when booking.

## 1. Listening and history

The visit starts with a conversation: how the pain began (a fall, childbirth, long sitting or no clear reason), how long you have had it, how it affects your work, sleep and daily life, and what you have already tried.

## 2. Examination

The clinician examines your lower back, pelvis and the area around the tailbone, checking for tenderness, swelling and how the coccyx and surrounding muscles respond to pressure and movement. Everything is explained first, and nothing happens without your consent. You can ask to pause at any time.

## 3. Pinpointing the cause

The aim is to find out what is actually causing the pain: whether the coccyx is moving too much, too little or sitting out of position, whether the pelvic-floor muscles are in spasm, or whether something else needs ruling out.

## 4. Treatment plan

You'll leave with a clear plan. Depending on the cause, this may include hands-on treatment such as manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles, together with posture and seating advice, a suitable cushion, and exercises you can do at home. Many patients notice a difference early, but the plan is always tailored to your own situation.

## 5. Follow-up

After treatment, a short check-in a week or two later helps track your pain and sitting tolerance, so the plan can be adjusted if needed.

## Book or ask a question

You can [book online](/book) at our New Delhi clinic or for a video consultation, or message us on WhatsApp if you have questions before deciding.

# Can Physiotherapy Really Treat Chronic Tailbone Pain Without Surgery?

Many people believe chronic tailbone pain automatically requires injections or surgery. However, a large number of patients experience significant…

Many people believe chronic tailbone pain automatically requires injections or surgery. However, a large number of patients experience significant improvement through **tailbone physiotherapy** and specialized rehabilitation. According to Dr. Rajveer Singh, identifying the mechanical cause of pain is the key to successful non-surgical treatment. [Tailbone physiotherapy](/) focuses on restoring normal movement, improving posture, relieving muscle tension, and reducing pressure on the coccyx, helping many patients recover without the need for surgery.

## Understanding Mechanical Tailbone Pain

The coccyx works together with:

- Pelvic floor muscles
- Lower spine
- Hip muscles
- Core stabilizers
- Sitting posture mechanics

Dysfunction in these areas can increase pressure on the tailbone.

## Goals of Tailbone Physiotherapy

Treatment focuses on:

- Reducing pressure on the coccyx
- Improving sitting tolerance
- Releasing muscle tension
- Correcting posture
- Restoring pelvic mobility
- Improving movement patterns

## Who Benefits Most From Conservative Treatment?

Physiotherapy may help patients with:

- Chronic sitting pain
- Post-traumatic coccyx pain
- Postpartum coccyx dysfunction
- Office-related tailbone pain
- Mild coccyx instability
- Pelvic floor tightness

## Importance of Personalized Rehabilitation

Some patients require:

- Manual therapy
- Pelvic floor relaxation
- Ergonomic correction
- Core strengthening
- Movement retraining
- Lifestyle modification

## Conclusion

Many patients with chronic coccyx pain can improve significantly without surgery through [Tailbone physiotherapy](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw) and functional rehabilitation. Early intervention and specialized assessment are important for achieving long-term pain relief, improved mobility, and better quality of life.

## FAQs

**1. Can physiotherapy cure tailbone pain?**  Many patients experience significant improvement through physiotherapy and rehabilitation.

**2. Is surgery always necessary for coccyx pain?**  No. Most patients respond well to conservative treatment.

**3. How long does physiotherapy take to show results?**  Recovery varies depending on the severity and duration of symptoms.

**4. What exercises help tailbone pain?**  Exercises are prescribed individually based on the patient’s assessment findings.

**5. Who is a good candidate for non-surgical treatment?**  Patients with mechanical, postural, postpartum, or chronic sitting-related coccyx pain often benefit from physiotherapy.

# Why Some Tailbone Pain Treatments Fail: The Importance of Functional Assessment

Chronic tailbone pain can be frustrating because many patients visit multiple healthcare providers and undergo various treatments without lasting…

[Chronic tailbone pain](/) can be frustrating because many patients visit multiple healthcare providers and undergo various treatments without lasting improvement. This often happens when treatment focuses only on symptom management rather than identifying the root cause of the pain.

Patients may receive medications, anti-inflammatory drugs, injections, or advice to use cushions. While these approaches can temporarily reduce discomfort, they may not address underlying biomechanical dysfunctions affecting the coccyx, pelvis, and surrounding muscles.

As a result, pain frequently returns once the temporary effects of treatment wear off.

## Common Signs That the Underlying Cause Has Not Been Addressed

Certain symptoms may indicate that the primary source of coccyx pain remains untreated:

- Pain that returns shortly after medication is stopped
- Persistent discomfort despite normal MRI or X-ray findings
- Difficulty sitting for extended periods
- Pain during transitions from sitting to standing
- Recurring episodes of tailbone pain after temporary relief
- Ongoing pelvic or lower back tightness

Recognizing these warning signs can help patients seek a more comprehensive evaluation.

## The Relationship Between Posture and Tailbone Pain

Posture plays a significant role in the development and persistence of coccyx pain. Poor sitting habits can place excessive pressure on the tailbone, especially during prolonged office work, driving, or sedentary lifestyles.

Common postural factors include:

- Slouched sitting posture
- Leaning backward excessively while seated
- Uneven weight distribution
- Poor workstation ergonomics
- Reduced core muscle support

Over time, these habits can contribute to increased stress on the coccyx and surrounding structures.

## How Muscle Imbalances Contribute to Coccyx Pain

The tailbone functions as part of a larger musculoskeletal system involving the pelvis, hips, lower back, and pelvic floor muscles. Tight or weak muscles in any of these areas can alter movement patterns and increase pressure on the coccyx.

Some patients develop compensatory muscle tension due to previous injuries, prolonged sitting, pregnancy, or chronic pain conditions. Identifying and correcting these imbalances is often essential for long-term recovery.

## Benefits of Early Functional Assessment

Seeking specialized assessment early can help prevent chronic pain from becoming more severe. A detailed functional evaluation can identify movement restrictions, postural abnormalities, muscle imbalances, and mechanical factors that may not be visible on imaging studies.

Early intervention may help:

- Reduce pain more effectively
- Improve sitting tolerance
- Restore normal movement patterns
- Prevent recurrent flare-ups
- Improve overall quality of life

## When to Seek Professional Help

Patients should consider professional evaluation if tailbone pain:

- Persists for more than a few weeks
- Interferes with work or daily activities
- Makes sitting difficult
- Returns repeatedly despite treatment
- Is associated with previous trauma or childbirth

Early diagnosis and targeted rehabilitation often lead to better outcomes and faster recovery.

## Long-Term Recovery Strategy

Addressing the root cause rather than simply masking symptoms improves long-term outcomes.

## Conclusion

Many [tailbone pain treatments](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw) fail because they focus only on pain relief. Comprehensive functional assessment and individualized rehabilitation provide a more effective solution.

## FAQs

**1. Why do painkillers not provide permanent relief?**  They reduce symptoms but do not address underlying mechanical problems.

**2. What is a functional assessment?**  It evaluates posture, movement patterns, muscle function, and biomechanics.

**3. Can poor sitting habits worsen coccyx pain?**  Yes. Incorrect sitting mechanics can increase coccyx stress.

**4. Is every tailbone pain case the same?**  No. Each patient may have different contributing factors.

**5. What makes personalized rehabilitation effective?**  Treatment is tailored to the patient’s specific dysfunction and symptoms.

Childbirth places significant stress on the pelvis and coccyx. While mild discomfort may improve naturally, persistent [tailbone pain after delivery](/) should not be ignored. Early intervention can help new mothers recover more comfortably and return to daily activities.

## Why Tailbone Pain Occurs After Childbirth

During delivery, the coccyx moves backward to allow passage of the baby. Excessive strain can lead to inflammation, bruising, or dysfunction.

## Common Symptoms

- Pain while sitting
- Discomfort during breastfeeding
- Difficulty standing up from a chair
- Pelvic pressure
- Persistent lower tailbone tenderness

## Role of Pelvic Floor Muscles

Pelvic floor muscles attach around the coccyx. Tightness or dysfunction in these muscles can contribute to ongoing pain after delivery.

## Importance of Early Physiotherapy

- Improving pelvic alignment
- Reducing muscle tension
- Correcting posture
- Restoring mobility
- Improving sitting comfort

- Physiotherapy
- Ergonomic modifications
- Activity adjustments
- Pelvic floor rehabilitation

## Conclusion

## FAQs

**2. How long does postpartum tailbone pain last?**  Recovery varies, but persistent pain lasting several weeks should be assessed.

**3. Can normal delivery cause coccyx injury?**  Yes. The coccyx can become strained or irritated during childbirth.

**4. Does physiotherapy help postpartum coccyx pain?**  Yes. Physiotherapy is one of the most effective conservative treatment options.

**5. When should I see a specialist?**  If pain interferes with sitting, feeding, or daily activities, professional evaluation is recommended.

# Tailbone Pain While Sitting: Understanding the Real Mechanical Cause

One of the most common symptoms of coccyx disorders is Tailbone Pain While Sitting. Many patients notice discomfort during office work, driving, or long…

One of the most common symptoms of coccyx disorders is [Tailbone Pain While Sitting](/treatment). Many patients notice discomfort during office work, driving, or long sitting hours, yet routine scans may appear normal. According to Dr. Rajveer Singh, tailbone pain is often related to abnormal pressure distribution, posture imbalance, pelvic floor tension, and coccyx mobility issues.

## Why Sitting Triggers Tailbone Pain

When sitting, body weight shifts toward the coccyx. If the coccyx becomes inflamed, unstable, stiff, or hypersensitive, even normal sitting pressure can become painful.

## Common Causes

- Previous fall or trauma
- Long sitting hours
- Poor posture
- Weak pelvic support muscles
- Childbirth-related strain
- Sudden weight loss
- Prolonged office work

## Why MRI Reports Can Be Normal

Many patients become frustrated when MRI reports appear normal despite ongoing pain.

This happens because:

- MRI is performed in a lying position
- Sitting pressure is not evaluated
- Mechanical dysfunction may not appear on routine scans

## How Physiotherapy Helps

Specialized coccyx physiotherapy focuses on:

- Pressure reduction
- Pelvic alignment
- Sitting posture correction
- Pelvic floor relaxation
- Muscle release techniques
- Mobility restoration
- Core stabilization

## Conclusion

[Tailbone pain while sitting](https://x.com/TailboneClinic) is often caused by mechanical and functional problems rather than major structural disease. Early assessment and specialized rehabilitation can significantly improve quality of life.

## FAQs

**2. Can poor posture cause tailbone pain?**  Yes. Incorrect sitting posture can increase stress on the coccyx.

**3. Is tailbone pain common among office workers?**  Yes. Long periods of sitting can contribute to coccyx pain.

**4. Why is my MRI normal despite severe pain?**  Many coccyx problems are functional and may not appear on routine imaging.

# Why Chronic Tailbone Pain is Often Misdiagnosed for Years

Chronic tailbone pain, also known as coccydynia, can significantly affect daily life. Many patients spend years seeking treatment for lower back pain,…

[Chronic tailbone pain](/), also known as coccydynia, can significantly affect daily life. Many patients spend years seeking treatment for lower back pain, sciatica, piles, or hip problems before discovering that the actual source of their discomfort is the coccyx. According to Dr. Rajveer Singh, proper diagnosis is the first step toward effective non-surgical recovery.

## Why Tailbone Pain is Commonly Misdiagnosed

The coccyx is located near several structures that can also cause pain. Because symptoms often overlap, many patients receive treatment for unrelated conditions while coccyx dysfunction remains undetected.

## Tailbone Pain vs Lower Back Pain

While lower back pain usually affects the lumbar region, coccyx pain is often localized at the bottom of the spine and becomes worse while sitting or rising from a seated position.

## The Importance of Sitting Pain

Pain that increases during prolonged sitting is one of the strongest indicators of coccyx dysfunction. Many patients report discomfort while driving, working at a desk, or sitting on hard surfaces.

## Understanding Dynamic Coccyx Dysfunction

In some cases, the coccyx moves excessively or becomes restricted during sitting and standing movements. These functional problems may not appear on routine imaging studies.

## How Physiotherapy Helps

Specialized rehabilitation focuses on:

- Posture correction
- Pelvic alignment
- Muscle release techniques
- Core strengthening
- Sitting mechanics training
- Functional movement restoration

## Conclusion

Many cases of [chronic tailbone pain](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw) remain undiagnosed for years because the symptoms mimic other conditions. A thorough functional assessment and personalized physiotherapy approach can help identify the real cause and provide long-term relief.

## FAQs

**1. What is chronic tailbone pain?**  Chronic tailbone pain is persistent pain around the coccyx that lasts for several weeks or months.

**2. Why is tailbone pain often misdiagnosed?**  Its symptoms can resemble lower back pain, sciatica, pelvic pain, or hemorrhoids.

**3. Can tailbone pain occur without injury?**  Yes. Poor posture, prolonged sitting, childbirth, and muscle imbalances can contribute to coccyx pain.

**4. Can physiotherapy help chronic coccyx pain?**  Yes. Specialized physiotherapy can improve mobility, posture, and muscle function around the coccyx.

**5. Does every patient with tailbone pain need surgery?**  No. Most patients respond well to conservative treatment and rehabilitation.

# How Can Tailbone Pain Add Limitations To Your Work Life?

Tailbone/Coccyx is a small bony triangular structure located at the end of vertebral column or the spine. It provides Support and Stabilize a person while…

## Tailbone Pain / Coccyx Pain

Tailbone/Coccyx is a small bony triangular structure located at the end of vertebral column or the spine. It provides Support and Stabilize a person while he/she is in a sitting position.

The **Tailbone Pain / Coccyx Pain** is the Pain and discomfort caused in the Tailbone area. The people with Tailbone pain have difficulties with prolonged sitting. They suffer from severe pain while sitting. This makes them ask for an official **[Medical Opinion](/doctor)** to get rid of the Pain and increase their ability to work. Since pain becomes an obstacle preventing them to work at their ease.

Some Useful Approach can be, Sit Stand Approach at your workstation-One can modify a computer workstation that raises or lowers as per your requirement during the office. This will enable you to stand and work when your tailbone is bruised or is hurting. You can then choose to sit down at workstation the minute you feel tired of standing and your legs and back start aching.

![Sit Stand Approach | Tailbone Pain / Coccyx Pain Treatment](/assets/img/blog/how-can-tailbone-pain-add-limitations-to-your-work-life-1.jpg "300x114")

This approach may not always work for all professions since the demands from the jobs can vary. For example it may not be appropriate to advise a person who is into a profession that requires them to travel throughout their day.

Similarly it may not be appropriate to modify few kinds of official work like in a Business Meeting where one cannot stand up in entire meeting when all other representatives are all sitting down at a table.

![Tailbone Pain / Coccyx Pain | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/how-can-tailbone-pain-add-limitations-to-your-work-life-2.jpg "300x114")

Most people may not be comfortable in standing throughout their day. And especially it becomes even more challenging for people who are suffering from Arthritis or any other pain in leg region such as knee pain, feet or lower back pain.

A person is able to sit and manage the whole day of work, if he responds very well to the treatment of **Tailbone Pain /Coccyx Pain** being given to him/her.

When the **Tailbone Pain /Coccyx Pain** worsens, people get completely distracted and are usually unable to sit throughout their work day.

Each person is different from the other. Every person has his own source of pain, severity of Tailbone Pain, response to treatments, frequency and severity of exacerbations etc.

It’s never advisable for a person to compare their conditions with other Tailbone Patients and take preventive measure on their own.

One need to consult a [Tailbone Specialist](/doctor) and take the right treatment to heal. Prolonged Pain in Tailbone makes it difficult for you to work and also brings in Emotional Stress.

So, an approach made individually makes the most sense.

# Bruised Tailbone: Requires Special Precautions. Slow to Heal

A freak accident or injury may lead to Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone. The coccyx, another name for the tailbone is situated in a medically…

Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone

A freak accident or injury may lead **to Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone**. The coccyx, another name for the tailbone is situated in a medically inaccessible place. It is located at the lowest portion of the back and comprises the last vertebral column of the spine. It is made up of 3 to 5 bony elements, which are held in place by ligaments and joints.

An injured coccyx or **Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone** can take a long time to heal. Hence, it takes longer to heal and requires extra care. The majority of coccyx injuries occur in women since they have a broader pelvis.

## Common Causes of Coccyx Injury

![Causes of Coccyx Injury | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/bruised-tailbone-requires-special-precautions-slow-to-heal-1.jpg "300x114")

### The most common ways to injure your tailbone are:

- Falling down in a seated stance, which impacts the tailbone the most
- Getting directly hit on the coccyx, for e.g. during sports
- Childbirth can also injure or fracture the tailbone

There are other, though less **[common causes](https://youtu.be/vm7BUchBp5Y)** of **Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone** injury like nerve root compression, bone spurs, injury to another part of the spine, local infections or even tumours. Sometimes, you may feel pain in the tailbone area without realizing it has been injured. However, you can still determine exactly where the damage occurred.

## Symptoms of Coccyx Damage

![Symptoms of Coccyx Damage | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/bruised-tailbone-requires-special-precautions-slow-to-heal-2.jpg "300x114")

Pain is the overwhelming symptom of an injured tailbone. The pain can be in different areas like:

- Pain or numbness while sitting down
- Tenderness or pain in the lower back
- Swelling or bruising at the base of the spinal cord
- Pain near the top of the buttocks
- Pain in bed while rolling over
- Pain while in the latrine
- In severe case the pain or numbness can shoot down the backs of the legs

## Medical Intervention

![Medical Intervention | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/bruised-tailbone-requires-special-precautions-slow-to-heal-3.jpg "300x114")

When the tailbone is damaged due to any cause, the pain will immediately compel you to see your Doctor. The first thing the physician will recommend is an **[X-ray](/blog/)** to confirm if there is a **Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone**. The first sign of a broken tailbone is pain when direct pressure is applied to it. Other reasons why immediate medical attention may be called for include:

- Pain, numbness or tingling in the tailbone area
- Swelling or pain in the tailbone region
- If the pain has been ignored but persists
- Weakness or shooting pain in the legs
- Persistent Constipation
- Issues with controlling bowel or bladder movements

If you’re experiencing sudden pain in your tailbone region only trained medical professional can tell you if the strong discomfort is related to the tailbone trauma or to a more serious disease.

A coccyx injury rarely requires emergency room attention, but timely medical intervention can give you the specialized care and treatment that a damaged coccyx or **Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone** demands.

## Healing an Injured Coccyx

![Healing an Injured Coccyx | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/bruised-tailbone-requires-special-precautions-slow-to-heal-4.jpg "300x114")

It takes a considerable amount of time to treat an injured coccyx or **Bruised Tailbone | Fractured Tailbone**, but even that depends on the severity of the damage. A fractured tailbone takes anywhere between 8 and 12 weeks to heal. If the coccyx is only bruised, it can still take about 4 weeks to heal completely.

If the pain and discomfort is not responding to treatment you may need steroid injections or even surgery to remove a portion of the coccyx. However, the last option may not be considered until 6 months post injury.

## Can You Speed up Recovery?

![Speed up Recovery | Tailbone Treatment](/assets/img/blog/bruised-tailbone-requires-special-precautions-slow-to-heal-5.jpg "300x114")

The patient needs to understand that whatever he or she does, it should not worsen the condition. He or she should consult a doctor, take it easy and give the area the chance to heal. It is important not to undertake any physical activity, which causes discomfort or pain. Resting is key to the healing process and the time it takes.

Do not take pain killers for the first 24 hours post injury, since the medicine tends to increase the chances of bleeding. Take pain medication as when required after 24 hours. If you have heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney or liver disease, have had stomach ulcers or internal bleeding at any time, confirm with the doctor that the prescribed medications will cause no further complications

It can be very painful when rolling over to get out of bed in the mornings. The technique is to move slowly and to get out of bed by pulling oneself into a fetal posture. Then swing your legs out in front but step to the ground slowly.

Avoid sitting on hard surfaces but do not sit for long periods of time even on soft ones. Make it a habit of sitting on cushions. You will need to purchase a gel donut or a cushion prescribed by the doctor.

Apply ice to the tailbone area for 20 minutes per hour for the first 48 hours post injury. However, do not apply the ice directly to the skin. After 48 hours of the injury, the patient must switch to heat pads, but should not heat for more than 20 minutes per application.

# Tailbone Pain is the Most Common Aches that Pregnant Women Experience Through out Pregnancy

Lets understand the basic of Coccydynia and causes of Coccydynia during pregnancy. Tailbone pain is the most common aches that pregnant women experience…

Lets understand the basic of Coccydynia and causes of Coccydynia during pregnancy. Tailbone pain is the most common aches that pregnant women experience through out Pregnancy.

## What is Coccydynia/ Tailbone Pain?

Pain in or around the coccyx at the bottom of spine is termed as Coccydynia.

## What are the Causes for Coccyx Pain During Pregnancy?

![Causes for coccyx or tailbone pain during pregnancy](/assets/img/blog/tailbone-pain-is-the-most-common-aches-that-pregnant-women-e-1.jpg "320x239")

Pregnancy hormones plays a vital role. During pregnancy, our body makes hormone called as Relaxing together with Estrogen causes joints and ligaments on pelvic floor to relax & stretch, allowing the coccyx to shift more than usual.

As pregnancy progress, the growing baby’s start pressing over coccyx which increases the pressure on coccyx bone leading to discomfort and pain in coccyx.

## How to Relieve Coccydynia?

Things to be done to relieve the pain are:

Meet a Specialist for Coccydynia in India for advice’s and measure’s to be taken to avoid further injury

www.Tailbonetreatment.com

a) Applying warm or cold packs over coccyx area twice a day.

b) Avoid long sitting and long travels.

c) Use Tailbone Treatment Cushion to sit (Click here to buy a certified Tailbone Treatment Cushion).

d) Frequently change positions.

e) Gentle stretches for the spine to increase mobility and relieve pressure off the tailbone under specialist guidance.

f) Postural correction through out pregnancy.

# Post Pregnancy Low Back Pain Could be Recti Divarication (Abdominal Splitting)

Diastasis Recti/Recti Divarication/Abdominal splitting is a midline separation of muscles of the abdominal wall. A palpable midline gap of more than 2 cm or…

Diastasis Recti/Recti Divarication/Abdominal splitting is a midline separation of muscles of the abdominal wall. A palpable midline gap of more than 2 cm or any visible bulging on exertion is considered as **Recti Divarication**. This separation is a normal occurrence of pregnancy, which is only a problem if the muscles do not go back to their correct position.

## How does it happen?

Diastasis Recti Abdominis commonly occurs around the umbilicus. It is a result of abdominal musculature stretch weakness from maternal hormonal changes and increased tension by the growing uterus. Diastasis Recti can occur in varying degrees during pregnancy and may not resolve spontaneously in the postpartum period.

## Why treatment of Recti Divarication is necessary?

Diastasis Recti (Abdominal Splitting) is commonly seen in women who have multiple pregnancies, which will make the muscles weaker.  This separation & weaker abdominal muscle can cause an array of problems, contribute to

- Back pain,
- Coccydynia/Tailbone Pain,
- Bad posture,
- Pelvic floor dysfunctions,
- Urinary Incontinence (Uncontrolled urination)
- Hernia,
- Cosmetic defects.

Back and/or pelvic pains are the most common manifestation of a Diastasis Recti Abdominis. A retrospective study done in 2007 by Spitznagle et al found that 66% of all patients with Diastasis Recti had support-related pelvic floor dysfunction (SPFD) diagnosis of stress urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapsed.

## How to diagnose this condition?

Ultrasonography (real-time ultrasound imaging) is an accurate method to measure rectus diastasis above the umbilicus and at the umbilical level.  A small separation of the midline at the abdominals, approximately one to two fingers’ width, is common after most pregnancies, and is not a problem. But if the gap at the midline is:

• More than 2 1/2 finger widths  • Does not shrink as the patient tighten her abdominals or  • A small Protrusion at her midline of abdomen then she probably have Diastasis Recti Abdominis and need to take a few special precautions during exercise and other activities.

## What is the treatment for Diastasis Recti Dysfunction?

Conservative management, such as specific therapeutic exercises directed by a physiotherapist, or health care professional well-acquainted with Diastasis Recti.Such exercises are aimed at strengthening the deep core muscles, such as the transverses abdominis and pelvic floor muscles. Poorly executed abdominal exercises can cause an increase in intra-abdominal pressure, this force may cause further recti separation and its accompanying bulge/hernia to worsen.

Hence, it is important to monitor Diastasis Recti Abdominis (and the hernia if any) before prescribing any abdominal exercises. Unsuitable abdominal exercises include sit ups, straight leg raises, Pilates movements i.e. “the 100s” and especially trunk rotation activities, such as criss-cross sit ups which target the obliques, can strain the abdominals excessively.

## What are the level of prognosis?

The patient usually does very well. In most cases, recti diastasis usually heals on its own over a postpartum period of 6 weeks to 3 months. However, Diastasis Recti Abdominis may also persist long after the woman delivered. Further intervention may be required if recovery of Diastasis Recti Abdominis does not occur. Specific therapeutic exercise may help improve the condition. Umbilical hernia may occur in some cases. If pain is present, surgery may be needed. In general, complications only result when a hernia develops.

# Psychological aspect of Coccydynia / Tailbone Pain

Dear Reader, in this article I would be explaining the psychological aspects of tailbone pain. I would be specific with the content and use simple words for…

Dear Reader, in this article I would be explaining the psychological aspects of tailbone pain. I would be specific with the content and use simple words for every reader to understand it. This content is merely understood by the general population, including health professionals. Tailbone pain occurs in and around the pelvic floor area, leading to symptoms like pelvic floor tenderness, buttocks pain, anal burning, and vaginal area pain (with pudendal neuralgia). I have come across a few male patients, who did not want to get married, only because they feared that this might hinder their sexual life. The fact is that, tailbone pain do not affect the male population, but the chances of feeling low after an intercourse due to the contraction of pelvic floor area can be expected.

Unlike the male patients, female patients with tailbone pain are affected as they experience more contractions of muscles and pressure on the pelvic floor after a sexual activity. It could become a nightmare with huge psychological impact, if the condition has occurred after marriage and if the couples are planning for conception.

There are a few important things I would like to share with the readers –

- Do not think that HE or SHE is trying avoid intercourse or ignore you by saying that they have pain around the genital area.
- Do co-operate and communicate with each other as this problem can happen to anyone.
- It is not a life threatening disease like cancer or AIDS, for you to be scared of. 
- After the right treatment you can live a complete normal life.
- A few months is all that matters during the treatment course, where patients have to be careful with their daily life activities. 
- After the right treatment a normal conception and delivery can be achieved.

Do not be afraid, help is always there!
